title: SPACE vs Primary Wave Music: Comparing Music Catalog Buyers for Independent Creators
metaDescription: Compare SPACE and Primary Wave Music for selling your music catalog. Learn how these buyers differ in deal size, genre focus, accessibility, and approach to catalog management.
introduction: Looking for Primary Wave alternatives for a smaller music catalog? Start with the rights you own, the income they generate, and whether you want a sale or a longer-term partnership. This comparison is published by SPACE, a catalog buyer, not an independent ranking service. Public sources checked September 7, 2026; no private offers were tested.
tldr: SPACE offers independent catalog owners a direct purchase review. Primary Wave combines catalog investment with artist and estate partnerships. Its public positioning does not establish a universal minimum revenue threshold or exclude every independent artist. For smaller catalogs, compare eligibility and written terms rather than assuming that the biggest company pays the most.

spaceProfile.description: SPACE reviews revenue-generating catalogs from independent artists, producers, labels, and catalog owners. Its published genre coverage includes ambient, lo-fi, meditation, electronic, house, wellness, and soundscape music. A review considers the revenue history, documented ownership, and interest offered for sale; neither genre nor catalog size guarantees an offer.
strengths: Direct buyer, without an auction listing process
Free application and initial review, with no listing fee or auction commission
Full or partial transactions involving defined catalog interests
No obligation to accept an offer
limitations: Individual review, not automatic acceptance or a guaranteed valuation multiple
An initial offer is not a promise of payment within the review period
A sale gives up the agreed interest and its future income; retained rights and duties depend on the contract

competitorProfile.name: Primary Wave Music
competitorProfile.description: Primary Wave describes its business around iconic catalogs and partnerships with artists and estates. Its services include publishing, recorded music, sync, brand marketing, and creative development. It also describes work with contemporary songwriters and artists, so calling it exclusively a legacy-catalog buyer would be inaccurate.
strengths: Catalog investment alongside publishing and recorded-music services
In-house sync, brand marketing, and content-development capabilities
Artist and estate partnerships extending beyond a cash purchase
limitations: Public positioning is not a published small-catalog acceptance test
No universal minimum, fee schedule, or closing timetable verified in the sources reviewed
A partnership needs a clear agreement on services, approvals, and economics

verdict: For an independent owner seeking a direct purchase, SPACE is an option to evaluate, not a guaranteed highest bidder. Primary Wave may be relevant when a broader creative or catalog-development partnership is part of the goal; confirm fit rather than assuming automatic rejection. Request comparable written offers for the same tracks, revenue streams, share, and duration. If the documents or economics do not support a sale, keeping the catalog is also an option.

bestFor.competitor: Owners assessing a partnership with catalog investment and creative or commercial development services. Eligibility must be confirmed directly.

sections.title: Primary Wave alternatives for smaller catalogs
paragraphs: SPACE is one route, not the only buyer serving independent creators. These alternatives involve different rights and income commitments. Confirm the current requirements before sharing documents or signing anything.

blocks.title: Duetti: purchases for independent creators
blocks.text: Duetti publishes master, publishing, and royalty-interest purchase options, including partial deals. Its offer page addresses creators earning at least $2,000 annually from their music rights and tracks as young as six months. These are Duetti's published criteria, not SPACE's, and do not guarantee an offer.

blocks.title: Limbo: catalog sales and separate advances
blocks.text: Limbo describes catalog sales through investor partners and royalty advances for distribution clients. Do not treat these as one identical product. Ask who purchases the interest, which rights are included, and whether the proposed funding requires a distribution relationship.

blocks.title: Royalty Exchange: marketplace price discovery
blocks.text: Royalty Exchange connects royalty owners with investors. Its guidance covers auctions and a 2020 introduction of non-auction Direct Listings; confirm today's eligible formats. Fees and commitments belong in the listing agreement, and its auction rules describe a winning bid as binding. A marketplace is not automatically slower or lower-paying.

blocks.title: beatBread: advance funding rather than a conventional buyout
blocks.text: beatBread describes its advances as limited revenue purchases, not loans. Artists retain ownership but commit defined income under the agreement. Fees, recoupment, the contractual term, and any new-release commitments matter; keeping ownership does not mean keeping all income during the arrangement.

sections.title: Prepare a smaller catalog for a useful review
paragraphs: A track count or streaming screenshot does not explain what a buyer can acquire. Assemble a concise package that connects ownership with the income being offered. This is a preparation checklist, not a universal eligibility rule.
items: A track list with artist names, recording identifiers, release dates, and the works or recordings included.
Your ownership share, collaborator splits, and whether the offer concerns masters, publishing, or only a royalty stream.
Available royalty statements organized by month and source, separating gross receipts, deductions, and your net income.
Existing label, distribution, publishing, advance, and sample agreements, including restrictions or balances that may affect a transfer.
Your preferred share and term, cash requirement, and rights you want to keep. Ask each buyer to quote the same scope.

faq.question: Can independent or emerging artists sell their catalogs to Primary Wave?
faq.answer: The reviewed public pages do not establish a blanket exclusion of independent artists or a six-figure income minimum. Primary Wave also describes working with contemporary writers and artists, although that does not promise a purchase of every small catalog. Ask about your specific rights and revenue profile rather than treating celebrity acquisitions as an eligibility rule.

faq.question: Does Primary Wave buy ambient or lo-fi music catalogs?
faq.answer: We did not verify a published rule excluding those genres. A genre label alone does not establish acceptance, rejection, or price. Seek a direct eligibility response and compare it with providers that explicitly describe services for your type of catalog.

faq.question: What does Primary Wave's active management mean for catalog sellers?
faq.answer: Its published services include sync, brand marketing, publishing, and creative development. In a proposed deal, establish which services are actually included, who approves uses of the music, and how income and costs are allocated. A service list is not a guarantee of placements, growth, or particular contractual rights.

faq.question: How does SPACE's approach differ from Primary Wave's for small catalogs?
faq.answer: SPACE's cited offer policy describes an individual direct-purchase review rather than a promised development partnership. It does not state a fixed minimum earnings threshold. Submit documented ownership and revenue for assessment; a smaller catalog can request a review, but acceptance and price are not guaranteed.

faq.question: Will SPACE offer 3x to 10x my annual royalties?
faq.answer: No fixed multiple is promised. Revenue history, costs, trends, ownership, and the interest offered for sale affect the review. Any calculator output or worked example is illustrative, not an offer. Compare the net cash and rights in written proposals rather than applying a generic multiplier to all future earnings.

faq.question: How long does it take to get an offer and receive payment from SPACE?
faq.answer: The published initial-offer timeline is typically 5-7 business days after the relevant catalog information is received, subject to review. That is not a guaranteed deadline from submission or a payment promise. Bank-transfer payment follows a completed agreement and satisfaction of the rights-transfer requirements.

faq.question: Can I sell part of my catalog and keep future work?
faq.answer: SPACE's policy describes partial transactions involving defined catalog shares. Specify the tracks, rights, percentage, and duration, and distinguish future work from the interests being sold. Have a qualified adviser review exclusions, approval rights, and continuing obligations; a partial sale is not a universal promise of unchanged control or income.
